extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political history and political theory (esp. histories of medieval/renaissance Italian civic institutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and evaluation of what constitutes a city, who counts as citizens, and which forms of government (and their corrupt counterparts) are good or bad, illustrated by Aristotle, Portenari, and medieval Padua's institutions. Includes institutional rules and eligibility requirements for councils and magistracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven necessary sorts of men for a city
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven sorts necessary to a city: husbandmen, artificers, soldiers, merchants, rich men, priests, and judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portenari (following Aristotle) enumerates seven kinds of men necessary for a city's functioning; he distinguishes between those who are parts of the city and those who are merely instruments subservient to uses (e.g., husbandmen, artificers, merchants may be instruments rather than parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for who are proper 'parts' of a city
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those whose operations are directed to virtue (especially wisdom and prudence) count as parts of a city; those occupied in mere labour or acquisition (husbandmen, artificers, merchants) are instruments, not citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: a city is constituted for felicity, and human felicity is in operations of virtue; therefore roles not aimed at wisdom/prudence should not be numbered among citizens. This is offered as a philosophical standard (Aristotelian) but is criticized as unjust and inconsistent with other principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property/independence as qualification for judgment and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A husbandman, merchant, or artificer who has any small property (so as not to depend for daily bread on a patron or master) is a sufficient judge of qualifications for representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portenari argues that a small property ensures a degree of independent judgment and will; property qualification is presented as a practical threshold for political participation/representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assembly as remedy for scale and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative assemblies remove many objections of representation in large states by enabling the body of the people to act in concert and have their opinions collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: direct assemblies of a capital are imperfect and prone to corruption; representative bodies are the only instrument by which the people's opinions can be known, united, and their strength exerted according to a continued system. This is advanced as the practical method for including diverse classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections of a house of commons to enfranchise middling sorts
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical method of giving farmers, merchants, and mechanics equal rights and proper weight in society is by elections, frequently repeated, of a house of commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portenari proposes frequent elections as a way to overcome the inattention of middling people to public affairs and to give them proper share and influence in the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a large middle state for stability and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: A free city's genius is to be composed, as much as possible, of equals; the greatest happiness and best preservation of equality occurs when the greatest part of inhabitants are in the middle state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: the middle state is most amenable to reason, less prone to the excesses of rich or poor, and best ensures safety and equality; scarcity of middling people tends to produce democracy or oligarchy and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three simple forms of good government
rubrics_metrics.description: The three simple forms of good government are monarchy (kingdom), aristocracy, and that which is called a republic/polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form is accompanied by its proper end and virtues: monarchy (one ruling for public good), aristocracy (rule by the virtuous and prudent), and polity (dominion of the multitude composed of all sorts and employed for common utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding corrupt forms: tyranny, oligarchy, democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: To each good form there is an opposed bad form: monarchy ↔ tyranny, aristocracy ↔ oligarchy, polity ↔ democracy (vile plebeians governing for private interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions and historical examples are given: tyranny as one who domineers for oppression (Phalaris, Dionysius, Nero); oligarchy as rule by the rich few who oppress the poor (Triumvirs example); democracy as rule by the basest plebeians for private ends (Gracchi example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy suitability condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarchy ought to be vested only in that citizen who, exceeding the others, is superior in riches, wisdom, prudence, and benevolence—almost godlike and devoted to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portenari (via philosophers) argues monarchy ranks first if the single ruler truly embodies supreme virtue; but recognizing such rarity, philosophers debate the practical preference among other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy vs oligarchy distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy is dominion by those adorned with virtue, prudence, and benevolence directing actions to the common good; oligarchy is a principality of the more rich and powerful who oppress the poor and corrupt the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocracy praised when magistracies and honours are in virtuous hands; oligarchy condemned and illustrated by Roman Triumvirs who proscribed citizens and plundered property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polity (popular government) vs democracy distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Polity (respublica) is dominion of the whole body—rich and poor, noble and plebeian—employing care and industry for the city's flourishing; democracy (corrupt) is domination by the most abject plebeians who govern for private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polity works by citizens learning from wise men and employing common reputation to distinguish fit rulers; democracy is warned against as self-interested plebeian rule that oppresses others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mixed governments and exemplary models
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed governments (combinations of monarchy, aristocracy, and polity) may produce ideal regimes (example: Lycurgus's Lacedaemonian model; Roman republic mixing consular, senatorial, and popular elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portenari notes several mixed types (monarchy+aristocracy, monarchy+republic, republic+aristocracy) and holds mixed forms can be among the most perfect when they select the good from the simple forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification and duties of the Anciani (Elder) council
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anciani/first council: initially 18 (later 16), three drawn by lot every three months (later 4 drawn every four months). No man admitted who was not a Padouan by birth, an inhabitant for at least thirty years, and having property yielding at least two hundred pounds a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties: conciliate/appease discord, oversee civil and criminal prosecutions, ensure decrees of the senate/public utility observed, maintain buildings/roads/walks, provide fire-preventing engines and equipment, read public letters from foreign princes and magistrates. Eligibility criteria and rotation/exclusion rules are explicit; used as instruments of general public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification and role of the Lesser Council
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lesser Council (initially 40, later 60) mixed noble and plebeian; matters had to be discussed here before being proposed to the Greater Council. Membership rules: rotation every four months, senators once served excluded for eight months; fathers/sons/brothers/uncle/nephew not permitted to sit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility: Padouan origin, father Padouan by birth, forty years continuous residence in Padua with family, estate of fifty pounds income, and prior submission to the offices of the commons. Decision rule: orations/harangues followed by votes; two-thirds suffrage determines questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and function of the Greater Council (Parliament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater Council: initially 300 senators (half nobles, half plebeians), later increased to 600 and finally to 1000 (in 1277). It chose magistrates and deliberated on all affairs relative to peace and war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two councils (greater and lesser) made municipal laws and statutes; copies of statutes were deposited in four monasteries by 1263. The Greater Council is the principal legislative/decision-making assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common council (open assembly) use
rubrics_metrics.description: A fourth council common to all the people, with open doors for anyone to enter, but very seldom assembled and only for matters of utmost importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the people's assembly in extreme cases; not a regular deliberative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podestà as remedial annual magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of an annual magistrate (podestà), a foreign person of noble blood and excellent reputation, entrusted with supreme judicial authority to govern the city and curb factional ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: instituted to remedy disorders caused by the consulate and extinguish occasions of ambition; podestà wields authority over civil and criminal judicial power and commands obedience from all magistracies and social orders as an impartial external head.
